places.name: Agadir
body: Agadir is a very different city, full of unbuilt areas, no actual Medina, and high speed winds which make the heat of the sun feel less aggressive.

This was (by far) one of the worst stops so far during this trip. I got food poisoning from the dinner I grabbed at the hostel, and had to stay in bed shivering with fever for one more night, until I was able to gather enough energy to keep going 😴

Let's also not even mention the fact that I was throwing up like crazy and had run out of drinkable water. And trust me, finding bottled water in a far suburb of Agadir at 3 a.m., while shivering from a 40-degree fever, is a hell of a challenge.
I can still feel the pain in my throat. Horrendous.
I also got a haircut (not the best, sadly), which I needed to properly survive the heat of the following weeks.
Finally leaving Agadir, feeling a tad better and most importantly free of fever and nausea, the bus is a tad late but that means it speeds everything up, which is great!

places.name: Akhfennir
body: Quick pitstop in a roadside trading city, where a lot of merchants and passenger buses were stopping for a coffee ☕

places.name: Atar
body: The heat is killing me, the sun is a literal laser and I'm running off roughly three hours of sleep, while I'm waiting for the next minivan to Tirjit, my bodily functions are slowly shutting down.
I did try to find a place with AC or a garden to cool down, but this city truly doesn't have this type of infrastructure...
A quick picture stop on the way back, with some beautiful mountain views, and the Atar plains in the background ✨

places.name: Bansko
body: A calm, small town nestled at the foot of the mountains, where fresh water flows through every little canal and along the crevices of the roads. It was a refreshing and peaceful experience, exactly what I needed after the intense heat of Sofia.

The streets are serene, lined with small houses and magnificent, lush gardens. In the evening, an opera concert enlivens the main square. I sit at the grand café, enjoying the view while planning my route for the following morning.

places.name: Barcelona
body: After some great mexican tacos and a couple of drinks at the Salts Montjuic bar, we went all the way to the top of the hill to camp in the forest.
Setting up the hammocks was surprisingly not as long as I'd have expected!

places.name: Belém
body: Stopover in Belem, passengers connecting to Manaus stay on board!
This truly does feel like a bus 🧐

places.name: Ben Guerir
body: A rushed stop in Ben Guerir, since we already were about 30 minutes late and the connecting train had been waiting for us.
I nearly missed my stop because I was busy taking stupid pictures 🫠

places.name: Benidorm
body: A quick pitstop in a lonely Spanish bus station, with some interesting lighting and a discarded motel vibe.

places.name: Benjamin Constant
body: Seven days later, our ship reaches the point where the Javary River merges into the Amazon. The original plan was to head straight to Tabatinga, but the crew is now considering a detour through Benjamin Constant. That would cost us an extra day and force me to reschedule my already booked hostel.
The hesitation comes from concerns that this particular branch of the river may be too shallow for us to pass.

As if to prove the point, we come across a much larger ship stuck in the middle of the delta and help move it out of the way. The roar and fumes of the engines make the whole scene feel far more dramatic than it really is.

After several minutes of mechanical struggle, the bigger passenger ship breaks free from its sand prison, and we are told to board it, since it will get us to Tabatinga quicker (this one won't go to Benjamin Constant, it wasn't able to even make it through the entrance of the canal).
I'm happy about the sudden upgrade!

places.name: Bogotá
body: Bogotá, the city of emeralds and constant autumn weather! I initially booked a cozy, modern hotel in the business district and was shocked by the high-tech amenities, jacuzzi, and spa.
I then moved to a more rustic place where many travelers would pass through and met some very sweet people from all over Europe and Latin America.
This city is frankly underrated. People tend to prefer Medellín over Bogotá, but I simply disagree. It feels so much more like it has personality
A rather tiring hike, but the view was worth it!

Montserrate towers at an impressive 3,200 m above sea level, making the ascent more of a challenge than your regular sea-level hill. The city stretches all the way to the horizon, and the vantage point is a perfect opportunity to capture some striking isometric shots.
Here we go, Colombia ends here, see you soon Bogotá 🛫
I do feel a bit sad about having to cancel my adventure through the Darién Gap, and directly flying through Central America, but it is for the best, and my partner needs support, so here I fly!
Lots of Colombian immigrants who live in the US on my flight, it's an interesting route because it feels demographically very different from the typical Europe-US flight.

places.name: Brasov
body: A charming small town nestled in the heart of the Transylvanian mountains, Brasov captivated me with its polished architecture, steep roofs, sunny terraces, and dark green forests.

For the first time on this trip, I was lucky enough to find some fun people to spend time with through the Hostelworld app. People usually do not reply in my experience. After a few drinks and shared stories in a bar, we all decided to go for a hike in Sinaia, a nearby village, early on the morning of 2 September.
The castle, as well as the view from the mountains over 2,000 metres high, promised to be worth the effort.

places.name: Bucharest
body: Drenched in sweat, dust, and a touch of blood (mostly for dramatic effect, after scraping my arms while foolishly reaching—several times, mind you—for some plums from a train window), I finally arrived in Bucharest and reunited with a friend. I could not help but feel a bit frustrated at having lost an entire day that could have been devoted to exploring the city and relaxing, but I decided to cut my losses and embrace the situation.

Our reunion was delightful. We shared dinner, sipped on rakija, and caught up on life, though sleep was scarce, as my friend had an early flight. After a few bus, metro, and car rides, I saw her off onto the train to the airport and then settled into my hostel.

Bucharest exudes the aura of a communist-era capital, full of monumental brutalist and neo-classical architecture. Yet what struck me most was how green and lush the city feels. It is a vivid contrast to the drier, more Mediterranean landscapes of the southern Balkans.

We returned to Bucharest after a nightly train ride from Cluj-Napoca, arriving in the morning. The journey was relatively short, so I fell asleep around midnight, forgetting that we were scheduled to arrive at 6. With barely 5 hours of sleep, 4 of which were likely very light due to the warm cabin, I wandered around the city like a zombie while waiting for my hostel to open.

Fortunately, after a big, restful nap, a nice soup, and a stroll around the centre, I felt much better and was excited about the next day. A friend from a past trip and I had agreed to meet up so she could show me around the city with her local insights.

I was able to catch up on some monuments I had missed during my first visit, as well as some brutalist highlights, all of which I have included in the pictures. I really think Bucharest is worth another, deeper look, and maybe a longer stay. Perhaps some volunteering in the future?

In the evening, we returned to the train station, where we both planned on boarding our respective trains: her to Pitesti and I to Chisinau. The schedule was tight, but we managed to catch the right trolleybus and get there with a few minutes to spare. The vibe aboard was legendary.

places.name: Cabo Pantoja
body: After a full day of high-speed navigation on the Napo, we finally arrive at our last stop: Cabo Pantoja!

I have to admit, I don't think I've ever been to such a remote place in my life. There is no connection to the outside world other than the river—no electricity, no wired internet, and just a few small roads, all ending a couple of kilometres into the jungle.
When we disembark, it's already night, and the hostel where I'm staying doesn’t have a generator, so everything is lit with candles. Quite a vibe!
Even finding a restaurant proves challenging since most people cook for themselves, but I managed to get my hands on some bread and a can of fish 🐟

I did oversleep in the morning and missed the boats leaving around 6:00 a.m. for Nuevo Rocafuerte, but luckily I found a backup plan leaving around 2:00 p.m., giving me time to explore the town and grab some breakfast with my host 🥞

places.name: Caïdat de Bir Gandouz
body: The Moroccan side of the border is pretty strict, they scan and search people thoroughly, and double check visas.
I met a polish guy there, he was coming back from Mauritania and heading towards the North! He had just been travelling by train from Zouérat and had a birthday party atop one of the wagons 🤯
Pretty cool dude, shame I didn't catch his Instagram or something...

places.name: Casablanca
body: Met a guy who knows the company I work for, the night I arrived at the hostel! Talked about it around a Tagine, and of course, took some pictures, because that is unlikely as hell.
Never happened in years of travelling 🤯
Obviously, a beautiful, gigantic mosque, palm trees everywhere, and tasty food all around the Medina. Coming outside of tourist season does have its perks 📈
The train got delayed by about one hour, meaning I had time to do some editing of some pictures I particularly liked, on a burning hot phone 🌡️
My Gandora truly allows me to breathe better in the AC deprived carriages of the train!

places.name: Central Macedonia
body: The city feels like time moves at a slower pace here. Life is unhurried, with a simple, rural rhythm. There are two small plazas where locals gather, surrounded by cafés and family-run restaurants, all reasonably priced and without any sense of pretension.

A friend invited me for coffee at the café where she works. We sat outside while the afternoon sun lit the square, watching neighbours greet each other and children play in the fountain. The next morning, she took me to a natural cave at the top of a nearby hill, a quiet and undisturbed spot. We got there on her motorcycle, riding through the warm countryside that opened up around us like a series of postcards.

We also made a spontaneous stop for karting, which turned out to be fun and quite affordable at about sixteen bucks, a good deal compared to home. This small city is a peaceful place where you can take your time and enjoy the days without feeling rushed.

places.name: Chinguetti
body: A chill pit stop in Chingetti to eat, visit the old town and the library, as well as prepare the necessary stuff to set up camp for the night.
The heat is honestly hard to bear, but the AC in the car helps.
We quickly climbed a massive dune before sunset and set up a tent at its top (don't worry, I wasn't only taking selfies; I also did help).
The view is magnificent, with sand reaching all the way to the horizon.
I ended up falling asleep a tad far from the campsite, waking up around 3 a.m. completely confused and covered in fine sand. 😭

places.name: Chișinău
body: Chisinau is this sort of town where, upon arrival, I felt like it wasn’t going to be a blast at all, and over time, with the help of a friend’s recommendations, and as my Russian was slowly getting less and less rusty, it actually became a very nice place to stay at.

The many parks, the lively streets, cafés, and the sketchy hostel with Ukrainian immigrants with whom I was talking in a mix of Russian and Polish, all of that, together made for a suspiciously enjoyable cocktail of experiences.

The mix of brutalist and classic orthodox architecture was a very enjoyable plus. I also did manage to catch up with a backpacker with whom I had hiked earlier in Romania! We got dinner together and exchanged recommendations around a couple of glasses of Visinata.

places.name: Choum
body: Barely awake and black from the iron covering my skin, I get off in Choum, a politically strategic and extremely isolated railroad city. All of the houses here are built using rails or railroad ties, to some extent.
Since I'm in a rush due to the train's multi-day delay in Nouadhibou, I decided to hop onto the next minivan to Atar, the region's capital city.

places.name: Cluj-Napoca
body: Cluj was the one addition to the list that I wasn’t entirely sure about, mainly due to timing concerns. It’s a lovely city with some beautiful Orthodox churches and vibrant city life, yet I didn’t find any highlights that made me fall in love with it.

The hostel was quite nice, and I enjoyed a couple of drinks with other travellers at a bar named “Toulouse,” named after Toulouse Lautrec, or so I was told. Unfortunately, I didn’t get free drinks for being born there… Disappointing, right?

places.name: Communauté rurale de Diama
body: A smooth security checkpoint, with an astonishingly low number of steps to go through (compared to Guerguerat or Rosso) and no bribery nor slow treatment.
The Senegalese police were quite nice and welcoming!

places.name: Communauté rurale de Diass
body: Around the world we go instead of following a simple straight line, because there aren't enough people willing to go straight from Senegal to Brazil 🫠
Also spending my last francs at the airport bar because they'll basically be worthless once in Brazil 🤷

places.name: Communauté rurale de Fimela
body: A cute little village next to the delta of the Saloum River.

I was initially planning on staying in Joal for the night, but the guide who took me in while I was hitchhiking recommended this place and even offered to arrange accommodation for me. The little houses are absolutely adorable and make for a great reading spot on the terrace during the heavy rains.
I am hoping to get an even better view of the delta tomorrow morning with a quick hop in a pirogue.
The day of my return to Dakar, I figured I could make a quick jump to one of the small towns located on the islands of the Delta, specifically Mar Lothie (pronounced "mar lodj").

The boats are all painted bright, with motives similar to the ones I saw in the Nouakchott and Saint-Louis fishing harbours; this cultural aspect seems common to most of the western part of the Sahel.
The ride is soothing, with some occasional tropical rain forcing us to get under a large plastic sheet which the pirogue captain deploys.
An extremely calm, and rather clean village, with some beautiful beaches, small houses, as well as a couple resorts on the coast.
A nice lady who rode the pirogue with me took me onto her horse carriage, which got me from the harbour to the town. The ride is bumpy but quite entertaining!
There is an immense amount of piglets roaming around the town freely, they are so cute!
Back to the docks after a couple hours having drinks with a view and some snacks in Mar Lodj, it's time to pack up and leave towards Dakar now.

places.name: Dakhla
body: Sadly my e-visa for Mauritania is taking some time to get approved, and I still feel a bit sick, so I've decided to stay here until I can cross the border safely and legally. On paper, this should allow my body to rest and heal, and me to explore the surroundings if I feel like it!
Update, 5 post arrival: the Mauritanian immigration authorities are completely incompetent and messed up my file on their systems, I have to redo everything all over again, morale is very low...
Update, 8 days post arrival: it turns out they mistyped my passport number, so the evisa was available all along, but I couldn't find it. This is just bullshit, I lost so much time here!
Luckily I had a contact in Mauritania who helped me speed things up, for free (beware of scammers who'll ask you to pay extremely high fees for their services).
I have never been so excited to leave a town in my life, Mauritania here I come (I am so glad this will be my one and only experience with e-visas during this trip).
The bus station layout was a tad confusing, everyone says different things about the time and location of departure, so I ended up going to the biggest one, and caught the bus on time.
A quick pit stop to buy water and food, the sun is still low, no sandstorm in sight

places.name: Dakhlet Nouadhibou
body: A sluggish process with a lot of fixers trying to get paid for the smallest useless service, some extremely rough and dirty facilities with not even a fan, smelling of sweat and unventilated air, honestly a hellish place.
The sand on the pictures has mines, by the way, don't go there if you like your legs 💯
Since the train arrived very late, most of the trip happened during the night.
It is a very intense experience, the sand is constantly blasting your face, following the turbulent air currents inside the wagon, and covering you up in a layer of black fine dust.
That dust also happens to be ferromagnetic, which makes it stick quite well to anything with a magnet in it 😭
But the starry night really was worth it, with so many shooting stars and extremely clear skies, with zero light pollution ✨

places.name: Dubrovnik
body: Landed in Dubrovnik in the evening, realised right after deplaning that the hostel was actually in a small town in the outskirts of the city.
Luckily I found a Colombian family who was kind enough to allow me in their Uber ride. The driver even offered to drop me off right in front of the hostel since it was on the way to his house!
The city's beautiful but the tourism is crazy, everything's overcrowded and extremely expensive, so I've decided to continue my journey on the next day, towards Mostar.
I drop off my luggage at the Bus station locker while I wait for the bus to arrive, and I get to visit the city in the meantime.
The bus is, obviously, late and I meet a group of people also travelling North, with whom I sit during transit.

places.name: Gevgelija
body: Why choose this small, forgotten roadside town, one might wonder?

There are no remarkable monuments, landmarks, or landscapes to distinguish it, and yet it felt like the right place to pause. After a thirty‑minute drive with a friend’s father to the border, the evening was already settling in, and the idea of reaching Skopje that night had grown increasingly unrealistic.

I spent the evening enjoying succulent peaches, cosy cafés, and warm pitas along the town’s main street, while preparing for the train I hoped to catch in the early morning. It departs at 4:40 a.m. from the central station. I can only hope the journey proves worth the wait. A simpler solution from Kilkis would have been to return to Thessaloniki and take a direct bus to Skopje, but this path feels more scenic, and I believe I made the right choice.

places.name: Gorna Oryahovitsa
body: I am using this stop in a railway hub in northern Bulgaria to upload all the pictures from the train ride between Stara Zagora and Bucharest.

I was fortunate to meet a group of Brits, along with one Irish girl if I recall correctly. We played cards, drank wine and beer, and their company made the journey far more enjoyable. I was lucky enough to run into them again later in Sighişoara, as they were heading there anyway.
I am really starting to love Eastern European trains, with their old and rusty compartments, wide windows, loosely secured doors, and tracks winding through endless stretches of lush forest.

places.name: Honda
body: A night in a small and cozy town, with some adorable hosts and an amazing, restful vibe.
The mosquitoes and the heat were clearly something I hadn't been missing, but the historical center and overall environment are worth the extra discomfort!

places.name: Houston
body: Early morning pit stop, and passport control in Houston. The United app sends me notifications every few minutes, closely monitoring my connection.
This feels about right; we're in the US, everything is somehow connected to the internet here.

The interesting part of this trip is that since both flights are rather short, we're flying A320s, planes which, as a European, I am used to seeing only on intracontinental routes. They are, however, equipped with in-flight entertainment, and we do get dinner, breakfast, and lunch.

places.name: Ibagué
body: This clearly will not be the most picturesque step, but I am posting it anyway for the sake of accuracy. I stopped there to split my bus trip to Bogotá in half, since the city is precisely halfway along the Cali to Bogotá route. I had some great pizza around the Airbnb I rented, but I forgot to take pictures.
My bad!
As I am writing this, I am working on gathering the pictures from Bogotá. It'll make up for this, promise! 🫶

places.name: Inal إنال
body: A warm morning aboard the Sahara express, with strong winds, black dust and a burning sun.

I truly consider myself lucky not to have stayed until Zouérat (I got off in Choum), since I would've had to endure the midday sun without any shadow, in a superheated box of metal running at insane speeds right through a cloud of abrasive sand.
Honestly, a spectacular experience, but not one I'd like to live through every two days. It truly is exhausting and intense!

places.name: Ioannina
body: A memorable lakeside city with very few tourists and a wide variety of cheeses, local dishes, and jewellery to choose from. In my opinion, this is one of the calmest and perhaps the best city on this journey.
The island on the lake is stunning. The rustling of the pine trees, the calls of the seagulls, and the absolute quiet of the lush Mediterranean forests create an exquisite cocktail of peace.

The hostel feels like a forgotten home, with an antique table standing proudly in the kitchen. Everything feels old yet familiar. I like this; escaping the busy beaches of Albania is an absolute blessing.

places.name: Ipiales
body: Right after crossing the border, I took a break in Ipiales, the closest city on the way to Popayan, allowing me to rest and to split the long bus trip in half, since it was already late.
It was rather cold, and the poncho definitely came in handy!
The city itself was not the most interesting, but it did reward me with some much-needed rest.

places.name: Iquitos
body: A pretty city in the middle of nowhere, supposedly one of the only towns of such a size with no road connection to the rest of the world!
The vibe's nice, you can buy drinkable coconuts on the street and the food is great, worth it 💯

I had to shorten my stay, sadly, since the transport options through the Napo don't run very often (on Tuesdays and Saturdays only). At least, the boat only travels during the day, which is a good precaution in those regions.

places.name: Jutaí
body: A 12-hour stop in this small town on the Amazon River, spent exploring the surroundings and buying fruits and drinks for the rest of the trip.
I didn’t know it yet, but because our ship was transporting a lot of cargo, these stops would become frequent after Jutaí, sometimes lasting 10 to 15 hours.
The Voyager V is not your conventional river transport vessel: it carries goods that are sold directly upon arrival at each port, which explains why the process was so slow.
Still, the food onboard was great, and having the chance to rest in a hammock all day during these breaks turned out to be surprisingly enjoyable.

places.name: Kalambaka
body: Giant rocky monoliths loom menacingly above a colourful Mediterranean town. Six monasteries float high overhead, as if suspended from the skies.
Μετέωρα is one of the most beautiful rock formations I have ever had the chance to visit.

The food does not disappoint, and the people are kind to us. It is a refreshing experience after Albania, Bosnia, and Croatia, where over-tourism has stripped away much of the warmth from the service workers we encountered.
I am glad I chose to take this detour on my way to Thessaloniki.

places.name: Konjic
body: A quick photo dump of the very scenic journey between Mostar and Sarajevo, aboard beautiful white Talgo carriages.
Mountains, rivers, dams, valleys and forests surround the track completely for most of the trip.

places.name: La Somone
body: Tired of Dakar’s noise, pollution, and high prices, I decided to head south in search of quieter, more affordable towns where I could rest while waiting for my flight.
La Somone and Saly are lovely places, popular with French visitors (mostly retirees) who spend at least half the year here. Hitchhiking between the two was surprisingly easy!
The beaches are beautiful, but restaurants and accommodations aren’t cheap, so I’ll be heading further south tomorrow in search of better options.
Managed to hitchhike all the way to Mbour! The town's nice, but the beach... wow, it's basically a giant plastic wasteland 😭
No swimming for me...
The town itself isn't that exciting, but I did stumble across a great restaurant serving insanely cheesy burgers and shawarmas!

places.name: Laayoune
body: Surprisingly, a rather modern and well maintained city in the middle of nowhere, with a very strong military presence.
This feels a lot like an initiative of the Moroccan government to properly affirm its presence in the Western Sahara by modernising it and building military bases there 🪖

The locals have been confirming that most of them come from northern cities, such as Casablanca or Rabat, but emigrated to Western Sahara following an expansion initiative by the Moroccan state, shortly after the well known "green march" (1975, the Spanish retreat from Western Sahara and Equatorial Guinea, Morocco organises mass demonstrations, supported by armed forces)

Sick again, with a cold as well as stomach cramps, I have decided to go wait for my visa to be approved in Dakhla, a bit closer to the border, in order to rest a little better and hopefully get fully back on my feet before I enter Mauritania.

places.name: Latour-De-Carol
body: Train station restaurant is closed on Wednesdays, so no lunch, hopefully we find something on the way 🤷

places.name: Leticia
body: Finally in Leticia, on the Colombian side of the three-country border zone. Warm tropical climate, a great hostel with a pool, and so many amazing people from all around the world: Switzerland, the United States, the UK, the Netherlands, Chile, you name it.
I’m waiting patiently for the next boat to Iquitos, though the schedules are notoriously hard to predict.

Immigration here works in a rather peculiar way: since there are no physical borders between the towns, you just need to get your exit and entry stamps at the right offices before leaving the city. Other than that, no major constraints!

places.name: Lima Metropolitan Area
body: Llamas, a dry climate and some very grey weather, the city where it never rains has a bit of a dystopian vibe, but it's culturally extremely rich!

places.name: Lisbon
body: Yeah totally on the way to Brazil coming from Senegal, right?
The absurdity of the modern eurocentrism shows in this scenario...

Strangely, my flight is the only one with a "via" subtext; the staff isn't really well informed about it, but it could mean that the flight will be stopping in Belem, then taking off again for Manaus, like a bus 🚌

places.name: London
body: A beautiful pit stop in the city of Big Ben with a self-transfer from Gatwick to Stansted, which cost me more than the price of the ticket to get from London to Toulouse. Thank the British Transportation System for its prices. Looking at the bright side, the weather was amazing, and I got to see most of the monuments I wanted to revisit.
Home awaits! I'm excited, it's been a while since I haven't been moving around every few days.

places.name: Málaga
body: I arrived barely rested in the morning, after a 10 hour long not-so-sleeper bus, and managed to gather enough effort to do a morning walking tour (coffee helped), but hey I made friends!
Málaga is real pretty, it feels like a seaside version of Granada, which seems coherent since they're both emblematic Andalusian cities.
Another great idea of mine: I decided to get to Tarifa by hitchhiking from Málaga.
After one unsuccessful attempt from a gas station near the Plaça Real shopping mall, I moved to the Arroyo de Miel highway stop (absolutely not reachable without some barrier jumping) and got lucky!

places.name: Manaus
body: The contrast between Senegal and Brazil is gigantic, I had almost forgotten how much I liked South America...
Beautiful, colourful cities, affordable food and public transport, lush jungle and magnificent trees everywhere ✨
Boarded and ready to go! The hammock ended up being crazy useful in the end, plus I now know how to tie the knots, feeling like a true local here 💅

places.name: Marrakesh
body: Last stop, Marrakech, all trains end here. The south of Morocco and Western Sahara can only be visited in bus, comfort not included 💅
Catching up with the guide from the last trip to Morocco I did! Super cool dude, excellent at his job.
Met with my friend from Marrakech, whom I shared a great lunch and night in the Agafay desert with 🌵
The beer sure was expensive but the views are worth it, only an hour away from the city!

Vibing to some traditional music in the car with my friend, literally saw like four crashes in front of us in one night... Marrakech is crazy dangerous for bikes, don't take mototaxis there, you'd be gambling with your life 🏍️
Left early in the morning, before the heat sets, to catch a bus to Agadir 🚍
The nice part is over, now the desert starts 😭

places.name: Medellín
body: Medellín? Honestly, yes, for the history and political influence, but living there? Never.

It's pricey, and a bit unauthentic: the brutal turn that happened in the last 20 years from hardcore criminality and cartel gun violence to the new, tourist-first industry has made this city unaffordable. Some comunas frankly feel like US neighborhoods, with Starbucks at every corner and hipstery restaurants everywhere.
I think it was worth the stop, but I wouldn't stay there longer than three or four days.
Change of plans here, I had to cut short my trip due to an emergency I had to tackle in New York, so I'll be flying out of Bogotá next week. Stay tuned!

places.name: Méderdra
body: Tightly packed on an overcrowded Jeep running through the Southern Mauritanian desert, we leave the main road to get closer to the Senegal river.

The Diama border crossing checkpoint is less popular than Rosso, meaning it is easier to get through if you don't speak Wolof or Hassaniya, and the police will not ask for extra money to get you through.
The road is however extremely bumpy and uncomfortable, I got there covered in sweat, and my back did hurt badly 😭

places.name: Mostar
body: Mostar is the first real pickle in this trip. I managed to find a last minute, rather expensive room in a nice residential area, but it is only available for one night, and since I plan on taking the morning train to Sarajevo, I must stay until the 31st.

This is the beginning of a long crawl under 40+ degrees of heat, a torrid sun, and with very little rest, to find an affordable accommodation. The excessive amount of tourists in this little town has completely saturated its hosting capacity, especially for backpackers.

Luckily, thanks to a local bartender whom Lies (one of the travellers I met earlier in Dubrovnik) and I befriended over a cocktail, I manage to get a hold of a nice hostel, where a no-show has freed up a spot.
I won’t have to sleep outside today, but Sarajevo will pose an even bigger challenge, as I’m about to realise.

places.name: Museo Plaza de Toros
body: After about two hours of riding through city buses and the subway, we finally made it to the "middle of the world," a tourist attraction north of Quito, located on the equator (to be precise, it is slightly off, but it's the thought that counts).
The park includes several artisanal shops highlighting local crafts from different regions of Ecuador, as well as some surprisingly inexpensive restaurants.

I’d say it is a good spot to cross off your bucket list, but a little overrated since there is very little to see around the park itself. It is, however, not very expensive and rather calm during the week.

places.name: Napo
body: These remote regions of the Amazon are known for being unsafe at night, with pirates occasionally halting ships and robbing passengers. Our boat therefore has to stop in Santa Clotilde for the night. This feels very far-westy, but it allows me to rest and resupply in a local pharmacy, so I'm not complaining!
The town is honestly worth it, very quiet and cozy with just enough infrastructure to not feel completely lost, including even a hospital.
I'm renting a room for 20 soles, less than 5 euros. It's no luxury but it is cheap and fair, and I feel safer than on our small boat in the middle of the night.

places.name: New York
body: A spectacular landing in LaGuardia, flying over Manhattan and New Jersey, quickly followed by a meet-up with my relative, who lives in Lake Grove, about 70 km away from the airport on Long Island.
Honestly, I expected this arrival to be a complete mess, due to how fast I had to plan it out, but it is looking great!
I meet up with my partner, and we spend some great time visiting the NYC classics.

places.name: Nikšić
body: This town was my first attempt at finding a place where I could finally rest, knowing that staying an extra night if I felt like it wouldn’t cost me fifty euros or more.
I had missed this feeling of freedom, which stems from the flexibility and financial independence one can only encounter in small villages and quiet towns.

Shortly after my arrival, I met a fellow traveler bound for the East, seeking refuge here while she recovered from a bout of flu. We spent our time together and wandered down to the lake; life was slow, and good.

places.name: Niš
body: Niš was not exactly the highlight of my trip, as I fell ill shortly after arriving. It is, however, a charming town, offering reasonably priced food and drinks, a large Ottoman fortress with well-preserved military barracks, and an intriguing underground Soviet-era shopping mall that tunnels beneath the main square and its surrounding streets.
I spent most of my time either in bed or observing passers-by from the terrace of a café, which hardly makes me the ideal tour guide should I ever return with company.
One detail that caught my attention was the frequent sight of military planes and helicopters flying over the city centre… perhaps there is a nearby base? I’ll take a look once I recover fully.

places.name: Nouadhibou
body: Quite a peculiar city, with no well-defined, traditional city center, and interesting no addresses.
When shipping something there, you'd usually just indicate the district, and the person would have to go to the post office directly to fetch the letter.

In all honesty, not an interesting city, but I stayed there to catch the train to the East, and it gave me some time to meet some locals and gather up some information about the political situation there.

Here I am waiting for a train with no precise time schedule. The Nouadhibou-Zouérat iron ore train Is one of the longest in the world; it transports iron ore from the Northeast part of the country to the northwestmost city, Nouadhibou.

A lot of locals use it to get through the Sahel more directly, since there are no roads that connect Nouadhibou and Choum directly, forcing you to take a costly detour through Nouakchott. Its legendary name "Train du désert" made me consider staying a bit longer to experience it 🚂
I'm hoping to get some good pictures, and to meet some friends who'll be travelling through the desert too, in their case starting form Nouakchott, further south!

places.name: Nouakchott
body: Finally in Nouakchott! The hostel's very pretty and cozy as hell, but the mosquitoes are a whole other story around here...
I've started taking anti-malaria medicine, just in case.

places.name: Paris
body: Tired but motivated, the flight is smooth as butter, and the attendants keep giving us free food. Air France is the best, I swear!

places.name: Patio de Comidas Baeza
body: On my way to Quito I needed a calm, rural place to rest for a little while.
I was looking for a small town in the middle of the jungle, with affordable housing and food, as well as beautiful surroundings, and Baeza was just that!
Magnificent cascades and rivers tearing through dense vegetation, birds singing day and night, highland haze covering the mountains, and soft sunlight bathing everything in a warm glow.
Honestly, I am so glad I stopped there!

places.name: Pikine Department
body: After prospecting for a couple days and running from one port to another, from peer to peer, and between bars, I end up figuring out that no amount of contacts will get me a ride in this season.
The current winds and hurricanes do not allow for a transatlantic travel by sailboat, and the cargo ships are not very willing to take passengers onboard.
After meeting with the chief of the harbour control tower in Dakar, and discussing ideas around an iced coffee, I came to the conclusion that it might be wise to book a flight just in case.
As far as cargo ships go, very few would be willing to accept a non-qualified member of crew and I'd have to wait at least a month and a half for that.
Therefore, I decided to book a flight to manaus on the 18th and finished visiting Senegal while waiting.
Back in the capital for merely a day, I got to meet again with my German friends from Guerguerat!
We were initially planning on visiting the island of Gorée, but the crowd at the port as well as our poor planning made me bail on it, since I had to get to the airport before 10 PM.
I did spend the evening at the arts village of Dakar, a beautiful, green and calm area where painters, sculptors and other artists display their work 🖌️

places.name: Δημοτική Ενότητα Ενιππέα
body: “On 5 September 2023, Storm Daniel triggered large-scale flooding in Thessaly. […] The line from Palaiofarsalos to Kalambaka was damaged, with extensive work required to repair the track and resume services. As a result, services between Palaiofarsalos and Kalambaka remain suspended across Thessaly’s coast until repairs are complete, with a rail-replacement bus currently in operation.”

Παλαιοφάρσαλος, a forgotten town among farmland, an improvised railway hub in the middle of nowhere, which we would never have even glanced at if it weren’t for this public transport hiccup. The station is new, yet unfinished and slightly eerie. Romani families shout and persistently ask us for cigarettes, old Greek men play cards, and the track lies quiet.
Around 8:30 p.m., My friend’s train arrives. She is headed to Athens and will continue solo from this point. Ours is scheduled around 9 p.m.
Thessaloniki is finally drawing nearer by the minute.

places.name: Plovdiv
body: Scattered throughout Plovdiv are numerous Roman ruins, Orthodox churches, and mosques. This city reminds me somewhat of Sarajevo; they share a certain ambience that I find difficult to capture fully in words.

Several churches rise above the old town, perched on the hills that punctuate the skyline. One of the best-preserved Roman amphitheatres I have ever seen flanks the main hill, blending the aesthetics of Ancient Rome with modern concert infrastructure and equipment.
At that point, I am unaware of this yet, but my plan to reach Bucharest by the evening of the 29th is about to backfire entirely. We will see how and why in Stara Zamora.

places.name: Podgorica
body: I am writing this about four days after reaching this city, and therefore am struggling to remember everything, but what I can say is that the train ride there was really beautiful, with lush forests surrounding the track at all times and cute little stations in the middle of nowhere, leading right into some small house’s backyard.

The city itself didn’t strike me as particularly beautiful or interesting, but I did visit most of the city centre, finally exchange my Bosnian currency for euros, and book a bus for the morning after to Shkoder (the train line is sadly abandoned and only serves some rare freight transport).

places.name: Popayán
body: This city surprised me very positively, with its typical Spanish colonial architecture and its location between two chains of mountains.

I initially thought that staying there on a Sunday would make the experience less enjoyable since many businesses were closed, but I was lucky enough to witness a Christian procession moving through the city, with children carrying musical instruments, statues of the Virgin Mary being paraded through the streets, and even the local news anchor recording an entire cooking show on the main town square.
Quite an experience!

places.name: Pristina
body: “A good city to live in, but not a good city to sightsee in,” the owner of the hostel told me. I respectfully disagree. As a backpacker, I’ve grown to crave these soothing, calm cities where not much happens and where local businesses don’t revolve around tourists, unlike on the Albanian or Croatian coast.

A magnificent Neo-Romanesque church stands at the end of the main street, and a beautiful modernist library—specifically late Yugoslav modernism—offers great photographic opportunities, especially from high vantage points like the church’s east tower.

places.name: Puerto Berrío
body: So my initial plan was to go east to join the Río Magdalena and then follow the river all the way up to Honda, where I could catch a bus to Bogotá.

Except my information was badly outdated, since people haven’t traveled this way for the last 10 to 20 years. Roads now provide a much faster connection. The only boats that still circulate are small cargo town-to-town hoppers, which don’t take passengers and move far too slowly.
I am sorry for the lack of pictures! I kind of forgot, not going to lie 🫠

places.name: Puerto Francisco de Orellana
body: After all this time cruising through the Amazon, Coca is the first city with a road connection to the west coast!
This is where my boating journey ends, and to be fair, I do not mind.

The slow boat from the border to here was actually quite uncomfortable: I expected a large cargo ship like in Peru or Brazil, but here it is more like a bigger, slightly slower version of the fast boats, with only seating, no terrace, few amenities and certainly no standing space.
I did regret choosing that option, but I guess you learn from your mistakes!
The town itself does not have any extraordinary points of interest, but it is still interesting to explore since it gives an authentic glimpse of the Ecuadorian lifestyle.

places.name: Quito
body: Really excited to be discovering the capital of Ecuador, especially since I'll be staying with the family of a friend I made in Senegal (who might even be reading this right now, since he's on Polarsteps too).

It's a bustling city, surrounded by mountains and valleys that give a unique high-altitude charm to the colonial architecture. I was impressed and pleasantly surprised by the modernity of the infrastructure, including the brand-new subway system, the business district, and the relative cleanliness of the streets.
The altitude (2900 m, up to 3300 m above sea level in the highest areas) did not bother me at all, which was great since we walked around so much. The sun, however, burned my lips pretty badly 😭
I am very thankful for my hosts, who were absolutely wonderful and helped me truly discover the city in depth 🫶

places.name: Rabat
body: Met up with some people I met in Tangier, who were travelling in the same direction as me, and visited the Medina, as well as the beautiful Oujida Kasbah by the sea. Absolutely worth it!
Leaving Rabat, waiting for my train at the nearby bar, where I met a very nice guy working for the Moroccan government, who gave me several pointers regarding Mauritania and its political situation ☕

places.name: Remanso
body: A slightly smaller-scale ship, a "lancha" as they call them here in Peru, not "bote" or "barco," which refer to bigger, open-sea ships.
The vibe aboard is sweet. Since I know Spanish much better than Portuguese, I was able to make friends with some locals—quite an important detail if you ask me!
The meals aren't as good as on the previous Brazilian ship, but they are still very filling.
This time, we carry cattle on top of the usual packaged goods and fruit, and I get to try a lot of different banana-based salty meals, which took me a little while to properly appreciate 🍌

places.name: Ripoll
body: Stopped there due to a technical issue, the stop was supposed to be 40 minutes long so I went out of the station to grab a sandwich 🏃
Guess what, ten minutes later, the train decides to leave and luckily I come back on time, but have to leave my beloved bocadillo de lomo since it was not ready yet 😭😭😭
10 bucks down the drain

places.name: Safi
body: Spent a really good time meeting locals, making friends and going to a big concert in the center of Safi, which apparently was happening every day during summer break 🕺
In the late morning, before my train, I explored the Medina (amazing Roman architecture and well preserved defense walls), as well as the local fish restaurants (I recommend the sardines 💯).
Literally melting from the humidity, heat, and heavy luggage combined 🤽

places.name: Saint-Louis
body: A very nice city by the Senegal river, with beautiful bridges and colonial buildings.
The weather was rather tropical in the beginning, but turned into some heavy thunderstorms around the end!
Of course, the drainage systems in this city weren't able to handle the sudden rush of water and half of the old city was underwater 🫧

places.name: Santiago de Cali
body: Now a brutalist interlude in Cali, the city of salsa. Despite not having a properly defined "old town" per se, beyond a small square with trees and churches, the city’s hills and markets have their own charm.
The brutalist architecture caught my attention and made for some uncommon shots!

places.name: Santo Antonio do Ica
body: A relaxing and very, very slow journey on a cargo boat sailing from Manaus to Tabatinga, the Brazilian city right next to Leticia, Colombia.

Our ship was slower than most due to its nature: instead of simply transporting goods, it was loaded with tons of random items (ranging from dog food to shoes, and even fresh meat) and sometimes spent more than ten hours at each stop trying to sell as much of it as possible to local merchants.
In a way, one could say this gave me more time to contemplate the surroundings. But in all honesty, when nothing’s moving and the sun heats the roof to nearly 40 °C, you do get bored pretty fast 😂

The cruise itself was deeply enjoyable, from the bar next to the small football field where locals played every evening, to the front of the ship where one could sit and enjoy coffee while looking at the water from above, or even the loud dining room, right above the engines, which drowned out any kind of human noise in a deep, reassuring roar 😌

places.name: Sarajevo
body: Sarajevo proved to be one of the most difficult places to find a bed in my backpacking experience so far. With summer being peak season here, as well as a big concert (Dino Merlin, apparently a star in the Balkans) happening during the weekend, not a single room, bed, or couch was available for me to book online. Luckily, after scavenging for a couple of hours, freshly off the train from Mostar, I managed to find a hotel that was only accepting bookings from contacts or directly at the reception. A huge relief, if you ask me.

The city has a real charm; the noise of the passing tramways, the small bridges jumping over the river, the lush forests surrounding it, as well as the countless mosques, minarets, and cemeteries, scattered all around the hills, give it a very poetic character. The old town is still a tad too touristic for my liking, but I believe its good conservation and cleanliness make up for it.

I finally get to try out the legendary Bosnian coffee I heard so many good things about (to be fair, it’s pretty similar to the Amazigh or Turkish way of doing it, with a traditional copper container being superheated on sand, but it’s definitely very enjoyable).

places.name: Saranda
body: A wonderful beachside adventure, though accompanied by a fair share of digestive trouble 💁.

There were clubs, bars, and plenty of swimming—both in the sea and, unfortunately, in my own clothes when the air conditioning wasn’t blasting at full power. A friend even came straight from Kosovo to meet me!
I had an amazing time. The city feels less like an off-the-grid, traditional beach town and more like a bustling tourist resort, but the classic holiday vibe was a nice change of pace.
As I write this, I’m still recovering from the five days of discomfort that followed, and my stomach has yet to fully stabilise. Hopefully, this will be the only such incident on the trip.

places.name: Septemvri
body: While most of the pictures here are not exactly from Septemvri, I will post them as a single step, with the highlights of the Rhodopes line: a beautiful narrow-gauge train winding through hills and valleys from Dobrinishte to Septemvri, where it connects to the higher speed intercity railway to Plovdiv.
A beautiful ode to slow travel and the nearly vanished rural door-to-door train systems.

places.name: Shalë
body: Finally, we’ve reached base camp… so to say, this isn’t exactly Mount Everest either, and yet it does feel like it, the beginning of an adventure!

As we’re having a short dinner at the restaurant, right after disembarking, I make an extremely unlikely encounter: a classmate from middle school recognises me, and we catch up on life over a sandwich. She’s also hiking around Theth, but only staying for the day, and leaving in the evening. I knew she was in Albania recently from our chat over Instagram, but definitely did not expect to stumble upon her and her partner randomly.

The chat ends, and time is running out, since we want to clear a couple of kilometres in order to set up camp far enough from Theth. After struggling for a bit to find the start of the trail, we get going.

We find a nice, flat spot where we can finally hang our hammocks, roughly half an hour before sundown. We have some dinner and go to sleep nearly immediately, since we’re planning on waking up around 5:40 in the morning.
The night is quiet and not too cold, with the occasional rustling of leaves caused by a hedgehog or a deer passing by being the only source of disturbance.
After countless struggles, breaks, mental breakdowns, jokes, and moments of amazement, we reach the highest point of the hike!

It is very dusty, and the sun is harsh, but several layers of sunscreen later, we take a couple of pictures. I climb the nearest peak to get a couple of selfies while my travel companion guards our equipment.
The view is truly worth it, but our destination is still so far in the distance! 🤯

We are tired, and every inch of our body feels sore. For obvious reasons, at this point in time, no pictures are being taken at all, so I only uploaded this shot of the valley. Your imagination will have to do the rest: we were making our way through the bed of the dried-up river and ended up reaching a farm, where a taxi was picking up two Italian alpinists.
We decided to ask them for a ride, which they kindly accepted, for about 500 leks per person.
We rejoice at the thought of finally enjoying a warm meal and a bed; the hostel is finally within reach.

A well-deserved rest in this isolated and peaceful settlement, where we finally get to enjoy some nice food and a good bit of rest. My travel companion and I are both feeling a bit sick, though, so we decide to go to bed early and hope for the best.

It may be linked to the water we drank on the way—one of the sources we used looked contaminated, and we only noticed after nearly emptying a full bottle of it. Hopefully, this is a basic bacterial infection and not some sort of parasite.
A quick pit stop while waiting for the boat to Koman. The weather’s great, and there seem to be very few passengers. I’d never mind a private cruise for a thousand lekë.

places.name: Shkoder
body: Shkodër reminds me more of a bustling South American city. It’s messy, noisy, bathed in an unforgiving sun, and its architecture is strongly anchored in the 90s, with hints of modernity in the centre.

The food is rather cheap, but the exchange rate from euro to lek is quite poor. However, I am not here for sightseeing: my friend has suggested that we visit the Valbonë Valley, passing through Theth (which we’ll reach by bus) and hiking through the Valbonë Pass (+1170 m of elevation gain, one of the hardest hikes I’ve ever had to do, especially with a 17kg backpack to make things even more challenging).
I need hiking equipment, and this city better provide it.

I’m not particularly in love with this city, and yet it seems I am coming back to it more often than I’d like. If it wasn’t for an errand I had to run before leaving for the south, I probably would’ve kept going directly towards Tirana. It’s very warm here, even in the evening, and I am already starting to miss the clean, fresh mountain air.
I will be leaving tomorrow for Sarandë to meet with a friend, so there is good news!

places.name: Sidi Kacem
body: A quick stop in one of the most important oil extraction and refining cities of Morocco, waiting for the connecting train to Rabat. The refinery, located right in front of the train station, really sells the industrial city vibe.
The heat here is really intense, more than 42 Celsius on the station's panels, with a strong, burning wind.

places.name: Sighișoara
body: I was told that Sighişoara was worth spending a night in, and it truly is. This enchanting town is one of the best-preserved medieval gems in Europe, rightfully listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

With no hostels available in the small town, I treated myself to a charming private room right in the heart of the city. My train to Cluj-Napoca departs the following day at around 1 p.m., giving me plenty of time to wander its cobbled streets, soak in the atmosphere, and enjoy a leisurely, relaxing stopover.

places.name: Sinaia
body: As far as mountain towns go, this one is surely among the prettiest. Most houses resemble royal mansions, and the train station’s dark arches and columns add to an ominous yet majestic atmosphere, reminiscent of the vampire tales we read as children.

The castle’s richly varied architecture and decoration are well worth a visit. I am glad I made this detour to see it. The weather was perfect for photos, with the low sun casting dramatic light and grey clouds in the background completing the effect.

After the visit, we hurried to the cable car station, only to discover that it was temporarily closed. This forced us to run downhill to the nearest operating station, as missing the next departure would have made it very difficult to reach the village before nightfall. We were planning to return on foot.

The views from the mountain top, more than 2,000 metres above sea level, were surreal and otherworldly. The hike down was just as rewarding, with light rain giving way to vibrant rainbows and clouds spiralling gracefully through the valleys. We managed to capture an incredible number of amazing shots during that expedition.

places.name: Skopje
body: A beautiful city, distinguished by its abundant neoclassical statues dispersed throughout the city centre. This unique combination gives the town a truly original character: Ancient Greek bronze sculptures stand proudly before stark brutalist buildings, with mosques rising in the background and monumental government edifices completing the scene.

The bazaar was a particular delight, feeling like one of the most authentic in the Balkans. It offers a subtle and captivating blend of the oriental charm of a traditional souk with the practical layout of a western-style flea market.

places.name: Sofia
body: Upon arriving in Sofia, my throat and nose were already aching, and speaking caused severe discomfort. I quickly headed to a pharmacy in search of an effective way to relieve my symptoms, as I wanted to be in Bucharest by the 30th to meet a friend.

After several rounds of anti-inflammatory medicine, antihistamines, and oxymetazoline, I finally felt some relief. I was then able to explore the city and capture some beautiful shots of this vibrant metropolis.
I was especially impressed by the public transport system and the many monumental government buildings that line the boulevards of the old centre.
The pictures speak for themselves.

places.name: Stara Zagora
body: What I consider the greatest planning catastrophe of this entire trip began with trusting a large language model to organise my train journey from Plovdiv to Bucharest. Despite cross-checking some sources, it provided me with outdated information from 2020, including a route that no longer exists.

Arriving in Stara Zagora, I confidently expected to catch the so-called “night train to Bucharest.” Imagine my shock when the ticket office clerk calmly informed me that no such train existed. The only option was a single morning regional train to Gorna Oryahovitsa.
With hotel prices starting at 60 euros per night and over 100 if I wanted to stay close to the station for the morning train, I chose to camp outside and hope for the best.

The night did not turn out any better. After setting up my hammock in a nearby park, I was abruptly soaked by a sprinkler system I had failed to notice. Drenched to the bone, I had to relocate. By 4 a.m., the temperature had dropped sharply, and the wind drove me to seek shelter in the station lobby. An hour later, a police officer nudged me awake with his boot, pointing me towards a row of small, uncomfortable benches I had avoided due to my height.
By the time I finally boarded the 9 a.m. train, I felt nothing but relief. This segment of the trip had gone spectacularly downhill.

places.name: Strait of Gibraltar
body: Strong winds and waves on the straight as I was waiting for my turn to get my passport stamped before arriving in Tangier 🌊

places.name: Tan-Tan
body: Arrived safe and sound around 11pm, to a very windy and sandy city, and a magnificent hotel. I was starving and was able to grab a late night pizza in the city center 🍕

The city is exactly what you'd expect from a town in the Sahara, sand, palm trees, harsh sun and camels. I had trouble locating the Central bus station since most locals weren't familiar with maps nor any other language than Arabic ✍️
Leaving the city of Tan-Tan to get to the next destination, Tarfaya. I'm super excited, it's finally starting to feel like an authentic trip through the desert 🌵

places.name: Tangier
body: Met some roommates right after arriving and went out for drinks on the main square, the Medina and Kasbah district are beautiful and full of vibrant colours.
It's finally time to say goodbye to the Mediterranean sea, I'm now boarding a train to Rabat, stopping at Sidi Kacem for a 40 minute break 🚂

places.name: Tarfaya
body: I stayed in the family house of a friend I made in Agadir, who invited me to spend the night there! Great city with some beautiful fishing boats and an overall calm seaside town ambience, was still feeling a bit weak from some low level sickness, so my energy levels weren't really optimal, sadly.
Found a taxi to Laayoune close to the beach, with some pretty views on Casa mar, the abandoned Spanish prison (fort Boyard vibes)

places.name: Tarifa
body: Sadly, the previous driver wasn't headed to Tarifa but to Algeciras, so here I am trying to find a new one, in a gas station near the city.
Visibly my luck did run out here, and I had to walk for about 40 minutes under a blazingly hot sun to catch a bus to the city center.
Found the bus! It led me to the central bus station, where city buses connected me to Tarifa.
Saved, finally 💪
After 40 minutes of bus from Algeciras, finally the African continent becomes visible. It's surprisingly reachable and close!
There are several cargo ships coming though the straight, with long trails of foam fading behind their hull.
Waiting for the ferry, grabbed a sweet iced coffee while watching pigeons and sparrows fighting for some pastry crumbs, wrecking havoc in the café
Airport vibes at the ship terminal, I missed the 5pm ferry but managed to catch a ticket for the next one, departing around 9

places.name: Terjit
body: I finally reached Tirjit after two full days and one night of travelling, allowing myself to relax in the hostel's pool, while I wait for my German friends to reach the agreed rendezvous location 🏊
The tents are comfy and there aren't many mosquitoes just yet; and the food is such an amazing reward 🥰
We get to visit the oasis adjacent to the camp in the morning, while nearly empty. The dates are sweet and juicy, the pool is refreshing and the surrounding area definitely is astoundingly beautiful!
In the morning, we visit another hidden gem of the region close by, Mhaireth.
Kids are playing in the natural pools, in between palm trees and arid sand dunes 🪨

places.name: Thessaloniki
body: The Marseille of Greece, if you ask me. This city has that classic Mediterranean low-key, cosy vibe I always enjoy.

Beautiful views, panoramic spots with sunsets over Mount Olympus, delicious food, and friendly locals – no disappointment at all. My Greek friends I met in Barcelona had praised this town, and I’m glad I came to see it for myself!

Sadly, I wasn’t in perfect sync with my friends because of the holidays around the 15th of August, when many people were out of town. That’s why I only stayed for two nights before moving on to Kilkis, where one of my Greek friends lives.

places.name: Tiraspol
body: In Transnistria (which Polarsteps does not seem to recognise as a separate country, unlike Kosovo), Russian appears to be the only widely spoken language. This makes things somewhat easier for me, as in Moldova, people sometimes expect me to use Romanian, which I do not speak at all. Some locals mentioned that the choice to use only Russian or only Romanian is somewhat of a political statement, reflecting their allegiances.

Tiraspol and Bender, two neighbouring cities, feature some timeless communist landmarks, such as a beautiful USSR-style communist canteen. Surprisingly, it is richly adorned with Leninist ornaments, a style I am accustomed to seeing in tourist spots. However, this place is entirely authentic, and locals actually dine there at a reasonable price (about 3 to 4 euros for a full meal).

places.name: Valencia
body: Real intense visits under a violent sun, the temperature didn't go under 30 during the night, but the city is gorgeous and definitely worth the night spent!
This was the last stop for my travel companion, now the true solo adventure begins 🤞
Time to catch the night bus to Málaga.
Cutting costs in Spain is key to avoid burning through money too fast this early in the trip.

places.name: Vau i Dejës
body: A little photo dump from the boat trip along the Drini. I finally reached the Koman Dam in the early afternoon and disembarked without any trouble.
The air was still pretty fresh, and I was only a bus trip away from Shkodër, where I needed to drop off some hiking gear I borrowed.

places.name: Yasuni
body: Finally in Ecuador! The border exchange rate was rough, but I snagged some dollars to keep moving.
The town is small, but its infrastructure seems more developed than Pantoja, even though they're geographically similar in size.
I'm heading out early tomorrow on the slow boat to Coca, so my stay will be short!

projects.title: Amaze.me
projects.summary: A two-dimensional maze generator and three-dimensional visualiser for the web.

cover.alt: A pink three-dimensional maze seen at an angle over a dark grid, with a small panel at the top left to set the maze size, toggle the wireframe and generate a new maze.

body.text: A web app that generates random mazes and visualises them in 3D, written in TypeScript with Three.js for rendering and Joy UI for its interface.
Using it
A small panel sets the size of the maze, from 5 to 55 cells a side, switches a wireframe view on or off and generates a new maze. The result is drawn as walls rising from a grid.
The app is hosted online, and the source can also be run locally.

projects.title: Avatar
projects.summary: A web-based SVG avatar generator that recolours a profile picture from a chosen palette.

cover.alt: A web page showing a flat illustration of a person with glasses in a rounded square, with controls to pick the shape, three palette colours, show or hide the glasses, then share or download.

body.text: A web tool for creating variations of one specific profile picture by changing its colour palette. It does not alter the avatar's design or structure: the drawing stays the same and only its colours move.
Features

items: Palette customisation: three colours (primary, secondary and tonal) that can be edited, locked or randomised.
Export as an SVG file, or rasterised as a PNG.

A preview of the avatar in three shapes: circle, rounded square and square.
A light and a dark theme.
