projects.summary: A simple and highly customisable command line interface for C++ applications.

cover.alt: A terminal showing the CLIfford prompt: a list of available commands, a greeting, and the program's name drawn as a large pixel-art splash screen in light blue on a dark background.

body.text: A generic command line interface library for C++ applications: you inherit from a base class, register your commands, and get a prompt with a history, a help system and a splash screen.
It is an archived project, originally built during engineering school at ENSEEIHT. No further development is planned, and it stays available for reference.
Features

items: Custom commands, arguments and options.
An integrated help system and splash screen.
Colour support, with ready-made helpers such as RED, GREEN and CYAN.
A command history.

body.text: Using it
A command line is a class that inherits from the library's CLI class and adds commands in its constructor, each with a name, a description and a function that receives its arguments:
It is built with CMake and needs a C++20 compiler. A demo program is included, and the library can be pulled into another CMake project with FetchContent.

projects.title: Cron
projects.summary: An Android alarm app that picks your wake time from your calendar, location, travel time and sleep signals.

cover.alt: Four phone screens of the Cron alarm app side by side: the home screen with tomorrow's 09:30 wake-up and a timeline, the planner's reasoning over the calendar, the memory notes, and the settings list.

body.text: An Android smart alarm that decides each evening when to wake you, from your calendar, your location, the travel time to your first commitment and overnight sleep signals. A second, fixed alarm is armed as a safety floor. The evening plan is computed with Anthropic's Claude.
How a night goes

Every evening, a daily trigger starts a session. Claude is given the wake window you allow, your travel and preparation buffers, your location and time zone, then works through a routine with tools: it reads the next 24 to 30 hours of the calendar, finds the first event that needs you somewhere, looks up its address, estimates the commute and sets the alarm for the arrival time minus the commute minus the preparation time.

The filtering matters. All-day events are ignored because they are markers, not appointments. Purely virtual events are skipped unless they are all there is. Back-to-back events are collapsed to the one that decides when you actually have to leave home. On a free day, the alarm goes to the latest time of a wake window you set.
Overnight, a foreground service listens to the phone and, when available, to sleep stages from Health Connect. A lighter model, Claude Haiku, is asked to re-plan when something changes:

items: If you fall asleep again after waking, the alarm is set again.
A short bout of activity in mid-sleep, under three minutes, is treated as a bathroom trip and ignored.
Ten minutes out of bed brings a morning briefing notification.
When the sensors show light sleep close to the alarm, it can ring a minute or two early to wake you gently.
After three snoozes, the app stops asking the model and simply rings again five minutes later.

body.text: Two alarms

The AI alarm is the one that moves. The hard-latest alarm is armed once, when the session starts, and never moves: if the model fails, the network is down or the API key is wrong, you still wake up by that time. The model can never set an alarm later than it, and the limit is enforced by the tool itself, not left to the prompt.
Under the hood

Written in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose. Each night is a session driven by a small state machine (planning, monitoring, awake, monitoring again, complete), stored in a Room database. Work is queued with WorkManager, commute times and addresses come from the Google Routes API, and the Anthropic key is entered in the app and kept in encrypted storage. Without a Routes key, the app falls back on a flat thirty minutes of commute.
The app also remembers things about you, such as how much sleep you need or how early you want to be at an airport, in a memory screen that lists what it has learned.

projects.title: Epidemic spreading
projects.summary: A graph theory study of the propagation of an epidemic, written as a Julia notebook.

cover.alt: A graph of about a thousand teal and orange dots joined by thin white lines on a black background, clustered around hubs: a network graph from the study.

body.text: A graph theory study about the propagation of an epidemic, in a notebook meant to be run with the Julia Jupyter kernel.

The notebook studies how an infection spreads over graphs, with models of the SIR family. It is run cell by cell, after adding Julia to Jupyter with the IJulia package. The cover is one of its outputs.

projects.title: ESP string lights
projects.summary: An MQTT-enabled controller for string lights with several effects, designed for the ESP32.

body.text: An MQTT-enabled controller for string lights with multiple effects and a physical button, designed for the ESP32, compatible with Home Assistant, and keeping its state across power cycles.
What it does
The lights are plugged into a relay, and the original controller of the string stays in the loop through a transistor, which lets the ESP32 trigger its effects. The board can be driven in two ways:

items: From the network: one MQTT topic switches the lights on and off, another selects the effect.
From the wall: a push button cycles through the effects, and the lights blink a pattern to say which one is now active.

body.text: The available effects are in waves, sequential, slow glow, chasing, fade, twinkle, static and a combination of them.
Hardware

items: An ESP32 development board.
A relay module that switches the mains supply of the lights.
A push button.
A transistor that stands in for the original controller's effect button.
A small mains adapter that powers the board.

body.text: Software

Built with PlatformIO. On start-up the board connects to Wi-Fi, then to the MQTT broker, subscribes to its two topics and keeps the connection alive, trying ten times to reconnect before giving up. Wi-Fi and broker settings live in a configuration file that is kept out of the repository.

projects.title: IPvChat
projects.summary: A C++ chat client and server infrastructure for Linux, configured with CMake.

body.text: A chat client-server infrastructure written in C++, split into a client and a server, both configured with CMake and built for Linux.
Client and server

The client opens a command prompt. Its commands let you test the connection to a server, connect and disconnect, log in with a user name and join a channel. The server is started with an address and a port, and prints where it is listening once it is up. For now it does not create channels or users on the fly, which the current architecture would make easy to add.
A session looks like this:

body.code:
ClientConsole> connect 127.0.0.1 8080
Connection successful
127.0.0.1:8080> login J0hn
Logged in as J0hn
J0hn@127.0.0.1:8080> join general
J0hn: Hey
Response: success OK

projects.title: ISF design system
projects.summary: A first draft of the design system of Ingénieurs sans frontières (ISF).

cover.alt: A Storybook page of a design system's colour palette: nine named colours, each shown as a row of ten swatches from light to dark, beside a navigation tree of components.

body.text: A first draft of the design system of Ingénieurs sans frontières (ISF), built with Next.js and documented in Storybook.

The palette is rooted in nature: ocean teals, sandy ivories and warm coppers, which echo the organisation's commitment to sustainable engineering in varied environments. Each of its eight colours (Deep Ocean, Forest, Ivory Sand, Golden Dune, Copper, Midnight, Sky Mist and Stone) comes as a range of ten shades, so that components, backgrounds and text all find a value in it.

The foundations also cover the logo and identity, radius, shadows, spacing and typography, followed by a library of components such as accordions, alerts, buttons, cards, modals, tabs and inputs, each with its variants and states.

projects.title: Lidar
projects.summary: A virtual reality game about escaping a maze you cannot see, using a lidar to scan your surroundings.

cover.alt: A dark landing page titled Lidar, a game where light is your weapon, over a perspective grid floor and grey hills, with a notice that a VR headset is needed to play.

body.text: A virtual reality game where you have to find your way out of a maze you cannot see: you use your lidar, a laser coupled with a light sensor, to scan your surroundings and avoid obstacles.
It is inspired by the Garry's Mod addon LIDAR by datæ, and is still in early development: playable, with many features missing.
The idea

In the addon, nothing that moves can be seen until the player has scanned it, which makes for a powerful horror mechanic, especially in VR where the scale of the space is so obvious. Lidar is also a real technology, used in autonomous vehicles, robotics and medicine: a pulsed laser and a sensor that measures the time the reflected light takes to come back, usually on a rotating platform to cover 360 degrees.

In the game, the module sits on the player's controller. An array of lasers is fired from it, and each pulse produces a low-resolution depth map. Combined with where the controller points, these build a point cloud of the maze, denser where you scanned close and sparser further away.
Playing

Point the right controller at a surface and squeeze the trigger to scan, release to stop. The maze is about 40 by 40 metres, and movement is not implemented yet, so you can only scan the part within reach.
Under the hood

It runs in the browser, written in TypeScript with React, Joy UI and Three.js for WebGL and WebXR. Points are kept in a fixed-length vertex buffer of 100,000 points, drawn as a point cloud. The ray casting that finds where each laser lands is accelerated with three-mesh-bvh, which keeps it fast on intricate meshes.

projects.title: Light engine
projects.summary: An inverse rasterizer engine demo in Java and Swing, extended with camera movement and a better interface.

cover.alt: A wireframe of a monkey's head drawn as a mesh of coloured points and lines, from green at the ear to purple at the neck, on a dark background.

body.text: An inverse rasterizer engine demo, written in Java using Swing. Most calculations run on the CPU, which limits performance, but it is a sample implementation of the rasterization process.

It is a heavily modified version of a rasterizer by C. Dehais, S. Mondet and G. Morin, with camera movement, further optimisation and a better interface. It was carried out as part of the computer rendering course at ENSEEIHT, and the code is not entirely the author's own, so care is advised before reusing it.
Using it
At start-up the program asks for a scene file; a few samples are provided, including the Blender monkey Suzanne and an A380. Once loaded, the scene is drawn as a wireframe, and the keys do the rest:

items: Arrow keys: move the camera around.
L: toggle the lighting.
Return: loop through the available shaders.
F1 and F2: wireframe and solid rendering.
F3 and F4: the same, multithreaded. These modes are experimental and turned out slower than the single-threaded ones.

body.text: Your own models

The scenes use a modified version of the OFF file format. A Python script converts a standard OFF file to it. Syntax errors in a scene file can crash the program, since very few robustness checks were made.

projects.title: Linda
projects.summary: A remotely accessible, thread-safe tuple database implemented in Java with RMI remote objects.

body.text: A remotely accessible Tuple database, implemented in Java using RMI remote objects. Mostly a proof of concept.
It was written as a team project, and tested on Java 17. There is no main class: the examples to run are in three packages, a prime numbers example, and a basic and an improved text search.
Known issues

items: The improved text search cannot use several searchers at once: doing so ends in a deadlock, which was traced to the centralised implementation but never fixed.
Stopping the server calls System.exit, which shuts down the whole process instead of only the server-side threads. Disabling the server timeout avoids it.

projects.title: Material sticky header
projects.summary: A proof of concept of Android's scroll-snap settings header behaviour in React and TypeScript.

cover.alt: A Storybook story of a mobile settings screen titled Internet, with a list of Wi-Fi networks and lock icons under a header that stays on top, beside an accessibility test panel.

body.text: A proof of concept implementation of Android's scroll-snap settings header: a sticky header that transitions between states with the scroll position, mimicking the native Android settings screen.
How it works
The large title of the screen collapses into a compact header as you scroll, then expands again, and snaps to one state or the other when you let go. It is built in React and TypeScript with:

items: scroll listeners that read the position,
transforms animated with Motion for the transitions,
a custom hook that observes the height of elements, so dynamic content does not break the layout,
state management for the header's visibility transitions.

body.text: The component is documented and tested in Storybook, with the settings screen of a phone as its demo story.

projects.title: Moneytor
projects.summary: A web app that charted your coding activity from the Wakatime API and worked out your earnings from an hourly rate. Retired when Wakatime restricted API keys to its plugins.

body.text: A lightweight web application built on the Wakatime API. It showed your coding activity in a simple way and calculated your earnings from your hourly rate, from the data the Wakatime plugins in your editors send. It needed a Wakatime API key, and at the time a browser request interceptor to authenticate, which was a drawback.

Wakatime has since changed how its API keys may be used. Its documentation now reserves them for those plugins (they are write-only), asks every other app to use OAuth 2.0 access tokens, and forbids a secret key in a public website's JavaScript. Moneytor ran entirely in the browser with the visitor's own key, so it cannot work under these rules; bringing it back would take a server and a registered OAuth app. It is no longer maintained.

projects.title: Joy UI palette generator
projects.summary: A procedural, accessible palette generator for the MUI Joy library, working in the OKLCH colour space.

cover.alt: A palette generator showing a blue seed colour, seven preset seed colours, and five rows of ten swatches (primary, neutral, danger, success, warning) with their hex and RGB values.

body.text: Generates accessible colour palettes for Joy UI in OKLCH, with gamut mapping to sRGB, WCAG 2.1 and APCA contrast validation, all five semantic palettes, and exports to TypeScript, CSS variables, JSON and Tailwind.
What it produces

From one seed colour, it generates the five palettes Joy UI expects (primary, neutral, danger, success and warning), each with ten steps from 50 to 900. The neutral palette is tinted toward the primary hue, and the semantic ones sit at fixed hues: red for danger, green for success and amber for warning.
How it works

It works in OKLCH, because equal steps in lightness look equal, saturation behaves the same across hues and modern browsers understand it natively. Each step has a lightness anchor, from 0.97 at the lightest to 0.16 at the darkest, and a chroma curve that peaks at the 500 step, which is the colour of buttons. Colours that fall outside sRGB are brought back by reducing their chroma while keeping hue and lightness.
Accessibility

The result is checked against the way Joy UI uses it: white text on the 500 step for solid buttons, the 700 step on the 100 step for soft ones, the 500 step on the page for outlined ones, and borders at 3:1. Contrast is shown both as WCAG 2.1 ratios and as APCA values.
Using it

The app previews the palettes with a button preview, shows the contrast results, then exports the theme as Joy UI code, CSS custom properties, JSON for design tools or Tailwind. The generation code is a small library that can be used on its own.

projects.title: Pconsole
projects.summary: A tiny, easy-to-use runtime console for Panda3D-powered applications, published on PyPI.

cover.alt: A Panda3D window with a Python console printing Pconsole's help, a command's usage and a task manager table, drawn over a television test card of colour bars and a grid.

body.text: A tiny runtime console for Panda3D applications. You give it a dictionary of command names and functions, a key to toggle it, and a command line is available in your running app. It is installable with pip install pconsole.
Setting it up

body.code:
import pconsole

commands = {"func1_string": func1,  # "associated string": function
            "func2_string": func2}
console = pconsole.Console()
console.create(commands, event="t")  # t toggles the console; f1 by default

body.text: Two commands exist out of the box: help lists the available commands, and usage gives details about one of them.
Reaching your app

projects.title: PyOS
projects.summary: An orbital mechanics simulator written entirely in Python on the Panda3D engine. PyOS stands for Python orbit simulator.

cover.alt: A close view of a huge bright yellow sun with a dark planet and a tiny moon in front of it, in a hazy nebula full of stars.

body.text: PyOS is an orbital mechanics simulator, written entirely in Python on top of the Panda3D engine.

It was created for a computer science class at PCSI Déodat de Séverac in Toulouse, and was heavily inspired by Universe Sandbox, a game by Giant Army. It was meant to become a sandbox space game and is now archived.
Where it got to

The last version, 0.10 alpha, has a new menu with 3D animations. The next goal was realistic impact particles, using the Panda3D particle generator, which would have paved the way for a proper heads-up display. 3D models can be imported and used in simulations, but there is no syntax guide, so it is hard to master. The project also reports its state through Discord rich presence.
Running it
Releases come as an archive with an executable that needs nothing else installed. To run the code itself, you need Python with Panda3D and pypresence.
The authors call the project officially dead and buried, and thank everyone whose feedback helped during development.

projects.title: Randomite
projects.summary: A pseudo-random number generator and visualiser for the web, with a gaussian generator and charts.

cover.alt: A page of random-number tools: a distribution picker, its formula and code, an AI-written description, and two charts of one thousand points, a two-dimensional scatter plot and a three-dimensional surface.

body.text: A web app that generates pseudo-random numbers and visualises them in several ways, with the ECharts library and Joy UI.

You pick a distribution, such as the Gaussian, and a number of points, from 250 to 2000, and shuffle to draw again. The page shows the generating function as code and its formula, then a plain-language description of the distribution written by a language model, and finally the points on charts: a two-dimensional scatter plot, and a three-dimensional surface plot, each with a short explanation of what you are looking at.

projects.title: Raycast capture and create
projects.summary: A Raycast extension that turns a selected region of your screen into a Google Task or a macOS Calendar event.

body.text: A Raycast extension with two commands: select any region of your screen and it becomes a Google Task (with an inferred title, note and due date) or a macOS Calendar event. The screenshot is interpreted with Claude Vision.
Commands

items: Capture to Task: draw a rectangle, and Claude reads it and creates a Google Task with a title, a note on the context and, if one is mentioned, a due date. It needs a Google OAuth client.

Capture to Calendar: the same capture creates an event in the Calendar app, with any calendar synced to it (iCloud, Google, Exchange), so no extra sign-in is needed. A default calendar is set in the preferences and can be overridden when the command is run.

body.text: Both need an Anthropic API key, entered in the extension's preferences.
Privacy and safety
Screenshots are sent to the Anthropic API and deleted from disk right after. Nothing else is stored beyond what Raycast keeps locally for its preferences and sign-in.

A screenshot is untrusted content, and a vision model can be fooled by text hidden in an image. The extension asks Claude to treat everything it sees as content to summarise and never as instructions, limits the length of what it extracts and removes control characters. Event data is handed to AppleScript as arguments, never pasted into the script. Above all, nothing is created without your confirmation, so the dialog is the place to check what was extracted.

projects.title: Slashboard
projects.summary: A dashboard to monitor the activity and performance of your home servers: an Electron and React desktop client, and a lightweight Node.js agent (Pulsar) on each server.

cover.alt: A dark dashboard for a home server showing its processor with core count, frequency and load, the operating system and uptime, a list of network interfaces, and the mounted disks with their usage.

body.text: A simple and convenient way to monitor the activity and performance of your servers: a desktop client built with Electron and React, which talks to Slashboard Pulsar, a lightweight Node.js app installed on each server.
What you see

The client keeps a list of your servers, each with an icon. Opening one shows its dashboard: the processor with its core count, frequency and load average, the operating system and how long it has been up, the network interfaces with their addresses, and the mounted disks with their size and how full they are. A switch hides volatile file systems such as temporary ones.
Setting it up

Install Pulsar on the server, make it reachable (usually with a forwarded port), then add the server in the client with its address, port and key. Hovering a server shows buttons to refresh, edit or delete it.

projects.title: Spectrum visualizer
projects.summary: A demo of a custom spectrum visualisation component for microphone recording interfaces.

cover.alt: A row of thin vertical bars in soft blues, tall at the left and fading to dots, drawing an audio spectrum, above a small panel to choose the variant, the colour and two options.

body.text: A demo application of a custom spectrum visualisation component: real-time audio visualisation from the microphone, with customisable colour schemes and a responsive layout.

The component draws the spectrum as a row of bars, one per frequency band. The demo has a light and a dark theme and lets you try its variants and colours, with options to interpolate the colours along the bars and to draw a faint ghost layer behind them.

The code is small on purpose. The component that processes the audio is one file, the amplitude indicators another, and the layout a third. It is released under the MIT licence, with a request to credit the work when it is republished without significant changes.

projects.title: Spinel
projects.summary: An OpenGL-based 3D rendering engine written in Java, created as part of the 7map project.

cover.alt: A red three-dimensional landscape of low hills rendered with simple lighting on a dark grey background.

body.text: Spinel is an OpenGL-based 3D rendering engine, written in Java and created as part of the 7map project.

projects.title: SVG gradients
projects.summary: A collection of experiments with grainy, noisy SVG gradients built on turbulence filters.

cover.alt: A grid of tiles on a dark page with grainy gradients: a pink to blue rectangle, magenta panels with start and end handles, a four-pointed star, a red flower shape and a grey tile with a speckled ring.

body.text: Experiments with SVG turbulence-based gradients. A LinearGradient component is a drop-in replacement for the standard SVG linearGradient element, documented in the source with examples.
A radial version works the same way. They give the grainy, noisy gradients that SVG's own cannot, by running a turbulence filter along the gradient, and the grain can be tuned and layered.
Examples
The demo shows what it can do:

items: a banner with a gradient background,
debug animations that show the turbulence field and its boundaries, for linear and radial gradients,
shapes such as a flower, a four-pointed sparkle and a torus built from several layered gradients,
text with a gradient fill,
compositions with several layers of different turbulence and colour,
an arch and an abstract piece that combine masks, gradients and shapes.

projects.title: Terrain interpolation
projects.summary: An OpenGL proof of concept of a procedural terrain interpolation algorithm, documented in French.

cover.alt: A white wireframe terrain with hundreds of red normal vectors standing off its surface, in a window titled Terrain interpolation demo.

body.text: A proof of concept for terrain interpolation, built with OpenGL, GLFW and GLM. The documentation is in French and most comments are in English.
The idea

The goal is to generate a terrain procedurally from a mesh of points of very low resolution, using surface subdivision. The plan was to implement Loop subdivision; for lack of time, a simplified version stands in for it: each triangle gets three new vertices, and a blurring pass then averages the vertex attributes to smooth the result.

Three stages show the difference: without any algorithm, the terrain is very angular and of low resolution; with naive subdivision it is just as angular but finer; with subdivision and blurring it comes out smooth. A high-frequency noise can then be added to imitate the irregularities of the ground.
Using it

The program shows a random terrain of ten by ten points, with its normals drawn in red. The arrow keys rotate the camera, Z and S zoom, and plus and minus raise or lower the level of detail, which is the number of subdivision passes. Faces can be coloured by normal and height, and lit with a day and night cycle.
The author notes that improvements are conceivable, such as simulating erosion or generating more precise textures and normals.

projects.title: Voxelife
projects.summary: A three-dimensional Conway's Game of Life in C++ and OpenGL.

cover.alt: Two clusters of grey cubes floating in three dimensions on a dark grey background, with a small colour axis between them.

body.text: A proof of concept of a three-dimensional game of life simulation, written in C++ with OpenGL for rendering.
Conway's rules are applied to a cube of cells instead of a flat grid, and each live cell is drawn as a voxel.
Controls

items: Arrow keys: rotate the camera around the origin.
W and S: move the camera closer to or further from the origin.
Space: play or pause the simulation.
R: reset and randomise the cells.

body.text: Dependencies are handled with vcpkg and the project is built with CMake, with a workspace for Visual Studio Code.

projects.title: Wave engine
projects.summary: A wave-motion particle simulator in Python, powered by Panda3D.

cover.alt: A square grid of small cubes seen at a low angle, with a ripple of bright red cubes rising at the centre, and a slider with rewind, play and fast-forward controls below.

body.text: A wave-motion particle simulator written in Python and rendered with Panda3D. The physical constants (rigidity, time scale, friction) are variables at the top of the code.
How it works

A grid of blocks pulls on its neighbours, with a rigidity and a friction, so that a disturbance propagates through it like a wave. Besides the three constants above, you can change the mass, the spacing between blocks and the global scale, and choose whether a stable frame holds the moving surface, which is worth switching off to see what happens.

The simulation can be computed ahead of time: a number of frames is precomputed, then replayed in 3D with a slider and play, rewind and fast-forward controls, which is how the user interface works from version 0.4. Live display is off by default, so that the calculation is not drawn while it runs.
Version 0.4
Added a dark mode, an improved interface, fixes for some rendering bugs and, most importantly, the precomputing, with a two-window interface. It is considered stable.

projects.title: Window controls overlay demo
projects.summary: A demo of the Window Controls Overlay API in an installable web app, for collapsing navigation bars into the title bar.

cover.alt: An installed web app whose title bar holds its own navigation tabs, showing a large headline about the web of tomorrow, a note that the browser supports the API, and an install button.

body.text: An experiment with the Window Controls Overlay API in a progressive web app, which lets a desktop PWA use the title bar area for its own navigation.

Installed PWAs normally keep a standard title bar. With the API, the content can cover the whole window, title bar included, as editors and music apps do. There are few open-source demos of it in React, and this project is meant as a reference implementation of a polished title bar.
Inspiration

The behaviour is modelled on the Vercel dashboard toolbar: a navigation bar that collapses and expands with the scroll direction, and does not snap at the first pixel of movement. A threshold, a kind of hysteresis, waits for a deliberate scroll before it reacts.
Techniques

items: The web app manifest asks for the window-controls-overlay display mode, and a hook listens to the geometry change event, so the interface always knows where the native window buttons are and stays clear of them, even when the window is resized or the text scaled.
Scroll-linked animation with Motion, driven by motion values that run outside the React render cycle.
A navigation bar that adapts to where it runs: a plain header in a browser tab, a themed title bar in an installed app, and a bar that extends into the title bar when the overlay is on.

body.text: It is built with React, Vite, the Vite PWA plugin, Joy UI and Motion.

projects.title: WhatsApp content moderation
projects.summary: A background-hosted "digital curtain" for a personal WhatsApp account: it links as a companion device, runs messages from chosen contacts through a local LLM classifier, deletes flagged ones locally and warns or temporarily blocks after repeated strikes.

cover.alt: A control page listing moderated contacts with counters for monitored, blocked, deleted and errors, next to a detail panel with strike counters, block settings and a moderation context field.

body.text: A localised, background-hosted "digital curtain" for a personal WhatsApp account. It links to the account as a headless companion device, runs incoming messages from an operator-chosen set of monitored contacts through an LLM classifier, deletes flagged messages locally ("delete for me"), sends a warning, and temporarily blocks a contact after repeated strikes. Repeated unanswered calls are handled the same way.
A web control app shows the moderated contacts, an activity log, the settings and the policy. It is pre-release: it ships with a shadow mode that only logs, and a live demo with invented data.
The classifier

Messages are judged by a local model run with Ollama, so there is no per-message cost and nothing leaves the machine. Each verdict is structured JSON: who the message targets, whether it is mutual banter and whether it is flagged. Banter, where the user teased first and the contact answered in kind, is let through, except for real threats, sexually explicit messages and pressure after a refusal. The last few messages are sent as context.

The classifier fails open: any error, timeout or malformed answer leaves the message alone rather than guessing. The rules are written in plain language by the operator, and small models follow concrete criteria much better than abstract ones, so naming the topics and the words to look for works, and describing a feeling does not.
Strikes and blocks

A flagged message is deleted, answered with a warning and recorded as a strike, once per incident. Reaching the threshold blocks the contact for a set time, plus or minus some random jitter so there is no detectable rhythm, then unblocks them automatically. Strikes decay with time, not with good behaviour. Each contact can be paused, unblocked early or given a stricter threshold, from the web app rather than through chat commands.
Repeated unanswered calls are tracked separately: past a threshold, the call is rejected with a warning, and a call strike counts toward a block of its own.
Warnings

The warning says plainly that the message was removed, that an automated system and not the account owner is watching the chat, and how many repeats remain before a block. It is sent from hand-written templates in English, French, Spanish and Polish, and an experimental option has a second model write it in the contact's own language.
Running it

It is meant to live on a small always-on machine, with Docker Compose, a two-core CPU-only box being the reference target. State is kept in SQLite, with a full audit log of messages and verdicts, which is the only record once a message is deleted. The control app is a React frontend served by the app, with live updates, and access can be restricted to one identity with Tailscale.

articles.title: Rendering techniques applied to caustics
articles.summary: A review of the techniques used to render caustics: texture projections, ray tracing, volumetric lighting, and real-time simulation as opposed to precomputed rendering.

cover.alt: A glass of water on a wooden table in black and white, casting a bright cone of light, a caustic, across its shadow.

body.text: Elliot Négrel-Jerzy, ENSEEIHT - Computer Science Dept.
Abstract

Replicating reality is a goal that we have essentially always been striving to achieve. This obsession with realism started with cave paintings, and has now reached the age of computer-generated imagery, with highly advanced, mathematically-proven methods, one of these being caustics. The existing literature does cover many approaches to this phenomenon, and their perks, including the following, which we intend to discuss here: we’ll explore texture projections, ray-tracing, volumetric lighting, and real-time simulation, opposed to precomputed rendering. Despite the variety of these subjects, this paper’s fundamental aim is to explain in simple words the idea behind these methods, as well as what makes them so effective.
Cost-performance trade-off

The most obvious distinction which comes to mind when talking about rendering objects, is between real-time and precomputed simulations. Both approaches do obviously offer unique advantages which are sought after in specific fields of computer imagery.

Pre-rendering, as expected, is not suitable for videogames, or any kind of interactive medium, since it consists of generating the images/video feed beforehand. This is done very often on a powerful machine, allowing for more complex and detailed simulations, while keeping the rendering speeds pretty low compared to what it would take for an average computer to do the same. Therefore, this technique is mostly used in cinematography and filmmaking, with software such as Blender 3D (open source), Cinema 4D, 3ds Max and many others (Fig. 1).

body.alt: G2 Crowd grid of 3D modelling software in summer 2016, plotting market presence against user satisfaction
body.caption: Most popular 3D Modelling tools in 2016, sorted by market presence vertically and user satisfaction horizontally (G2, 2016)

body.text: In contrast, real-time rendering techniques are extensively becoming the preferred method for 3D imagery (Christen, 2017), due to their speed, which allows for an efficient workflow, and a quick visualisation of the final result. Now, obviously, this speed doesn’t come without a cost: accuracy is considered low priority, hence algorithms which require heavy computations will often be replaced with visually similar, although physically incorrect alternatives.

However, it is important to note that nowadays, the frontier between these two categories is becoming thinner with the constant increase in computing power, and the new algorithms made available on the market (cf. Unreal Engine 5 – Lumen Global Illumination and Reflections). On the same note, software usually used in pre-computed rendering can be applied to virtual reality, and other forms of interactive 3D visualization in some very specific hardware configurations (Interactive rendering with blender cycles for virtual reality using hpc clusters, 2019), such as the one described below (Fig. 2). Here, the computing power is fully relocated to a high-performance computing data centre, which can handle the rendering of 60 images in one second. This cloud-computing infrastructure receives lightweight network packets containing user input data, and sends back compressed images back to the user’s interface.

body.alt: Diagram of a Blender visualisation client connected to a high-performance computing cluster for distributed rendering
body.caption: Cloud-computing infrastructure, featuring an HPC distributed rendering Cluster (Interactive rendering with blender cycles for virtual reality using hpc clusters, 2019)

body.text: Caustic Rendering

Now that we have properly defined the technical solutions used in the field of computer-generated imagery, we can finally explore in detail what Caustics are, and how most render engines approach them.

Caustic networks are shapes of concentrated light projected onto a surface, which are created when rays of light pass through a curved object made of a transparent material. A common occurrence of these optic artefacts is a glass of water exposed to a powerful light source (Fig. 3). Again, various methods are available. The most naïve approach uses ray-tracing (Wyman, et al., 2004) to calculate the colour of each pixel of the image. To keep things simple, it can be summarized in the following manner: the computer casts a ray from each pixel of the camera, which intersects both the pixel of the near plane¹ (see Fig. 4) and the eye point (centre of the projection). This ray then bounces off the faces of the objects it encounters, or gets through them, following the basic principles of refraction and reflection angles; throughout this process, it gains or loses energy, as the surfaces it hits absorb part of it. The ray will keep on bouncing until a maximum number of iterations (set by the user) is reached. If by then it has not collided with a light source, the pixel will be black, or else it will inherit the light source’s colour (this is a clear oversimplification of the process, if you want to know more about it, please check the bibliography (Arvo, 1986)).

¹ The near plane, or near clipping plane lies perpendicular to the camera direction. The distance from the camera (eye point) to the near plane is the closest distance that any object can be to the camera while still remaining in the view.

body.alt: A glass of water casting a bright caustic pattern on a surface
body.caption: Caustics created by a glass of water (cgiknowledge, 2013)

body.alt: Diagram of a virtual camera showing the near and far clipping planes and the field of view
body.caption: Common representation of a virtual camera in 3D rendering (Moccozet, 2008)

body.text: This approach is efficient, but as you might have guessed by now, extremely costly and slow. Hence, the preferred technique in the video game and virtual/augmented reality industry, attempts to replace most of these heavy calculations with pre-computed models (Zeltner, et al., 2020), at the expense of accuracy. This sacrifice is however absolutely legitimate, since as long as the player does not physically interact with the shape of the object through which light shines, there is no reason for the game to recompute the aforementioned model in real-time.

A common example (Dual Heights Software AB, 2021) of its use is water: pre-calculated caustics textures are projected onto the ocean/pool floor (Fig. 5) and distorted to create the illusion of movement, while the water surface itself is displaced according to an independent noise texture. The lack of consistency between cause (distortion of the water surface) and effect (resulting caustic network) remains unnoticed as long as the waves are low in height and uniform.

body.alt: Caustic network textures projected onto a cylinder, a sphere and a cube in Unity
body.caption: Caustic network textures projected onto various shapes in Unity 3D (Dual Heights Software AB, 2021)

body.text: More complex situations, such as moving glass surfaces or dynamic bodies of water, require more advanced models (Villani, 2009), which allow the algorithm to avoid using actual ray-tracing, and still get significantly convincing results.
Conclusion

With the increasing presence of virtual and augmented reality in our lives on a daily basis, computer graphics have become a major part of our lives, and before we know it, we might as well end up spending more time in simulated environments than in our actual world. Thus, the breakthroughs made in the field of lighting, and more specifically caustics are more than necessary, they are vital to our mental health in the long run. Despite the fact that at this point, we still need to use smart tricks (Xiao, et al., 2020) to get away with the extensive complexity and cost of our algorithms, it is safe to assume that, in a couple years, we’ll have sorted these issues out, either by improving our hardware or by creating new, more efficient software solutions.

articles.title: Virtual reality technologies
articles.summary: A comparison of the hardware, tracking systems and software behind virtual reality headsets, summarising the available literature.

cover.alt: An exploded diagram of an Oculus Rift headset labelling its cover, circuit board, display, lenses and foam padding, with the view each eye receives.

body.text: Elliot Négrel-Jerzy, ENSEEIHT - Computer Science Dept.
Abstract

Virtual reality, a dream become reality, a software marvel combined with decades of experience in computer hardware, sensors, but also, most importantly a tool, now used in a large variety of domains. Although at first sight, the concept might seem easy to get a grasp of, the technology behind it is considerably more complex than one might think at first sight. The available literature is extremely detailed and comprehensive; therefore, this article’s aim is to compare and summarize in a clear and concise manner the many approaches chosen to address the subject. We’ll be exploring the existing hardware, as well as the most commonly used tracking systems and the software bringing this whole machinery to life.
VR display hardware solutions

The state-of-the-art virtual reality headsets available on the market have led major companies such as Meta or Google to seriously consider investing in this domain, despite the initial drawbacks that the new technology came with. Their interest is, to this day, one of the main reasons why these devices are being mass produced, and are as a result, substantially cheap.

After taking a look at the actual design of one of these headsets (Parkin, 2014), we can identify three “main” components, the first being the circuit board. It features a highly powerful graphical processing unit, due to the very high requirements in terms of display latency: extended looking at a slow and unresponsive video feed has proven to induce nausea and headaches.

body.alt: Exploded view of an Oculus Rift headset showing the foam padding, lenses, display, circuit board and cover
body.caption: Inside view of an Oculus Rift VR headset (Parkin, 2014)

body.text: This board is then connected to a high-definition display module, whose technology can vary depending on the budget (LCD or OLED solutions are often preferred). However, the most commonly encountered design uses a backlit liquid crystal display, i.e., a non-emissive, translucent layer of so-called liquid crystals (extensively small cells whose color can be dynamically changed by applying a specific voltage for each color), coupled with a monochrome light-emitting backlight unit (BLU), which ensured the visibility of the content displayed on the aforementioned layer, by shining light through it.

body.alt: Layered schematic of a liquid crystal display: polarising filters, colour filters, liquid crystal layer, TFT array and backlight
body.caption: Schematic diagram of an LCD (Liquid crystal display and organic light-emitting diode display: present status and future perspectives, 2017)

body.text: Finally, two lenses are positioned in front of both eyes, ensuring that the perceived image is positioned “at infinity”, so as to reduce eye strain. This setting essentially means that the light coming from the objects as seen through the lens will appear to be coming from a very long distance, thus allowing the user’s eyes to effortlessly focus on them.
At this point, we do have a fairly accurate view of how an average entry-level VR headset’s works; therefore, we can dive into the existing hardware solutions used in movement and position tracking.
Tracking systems

Presently, virtual reality is being used in a plethora of domains, most of which require an interaction between the user and the virtual environment in which he is immersed, hence the necessity of tracking movement and position in space, sometimes even to the accuracy level of finger movement.

Multiple solutions do exist, and yet it would be a lie to say that these are in competition on the market, as each and every single one of them is more suitable for certain specific use cases. Open environments with great freedom of movement, such as virtual reality battle arenas (e.g., EVA) or military combat training infrastructure (Lele, 2011), will require positional tracking of limbs and weapons, which best works using optical tracking methods. The monitored zone cannot be infinite, and must be surrounded with cameras, coupled with highly powerful light projectors (preferably infrared, due to its imperceptibility to the human eye). The user should be equipped with judiciously placed retro-reflective markers, so as to minimize the positional estimation error; obviously, these markers are in general specifically designed to reflect extremely well the light frequency emitted by the aforementioned projectors. In the end, what the cameras see is an extremely dark image, covered with blindingly white dots, which correspond to the limbs of the user, and whose coordinates can later be determined, in order to programmatically calculate his position. Variations of this method may involve laser emitters instead of markers (Simulation of a virtual reality tracking system, 2011), whose beams will project dots of light on the walls of the monitored room. However, both techniques make use of cameras when it comes to locating them.

body.alt: Diagram of a retro-reflective optical tracking system with three panels showing how markers are detected
body.caption: Visualization of an optical tracker's detection system (RetroTracker: Upgrading Existing Virtual Reality Tracking Systems, 2019)

body.text: High precision motion capture is usually sought after in VR apps which call for (included but not limited to) hand-gesture detection and close contact interactions with the environment. Again, several solutions are available to the public: optical detection in conjunction with AI algorithms, or gloves/suits equipped with structural deformation sensors.

body.alt: A motion capture room where a person wears a marker suit and gloves fitted with tracking markers
body.caption: Motion capture using an Optitrack marker suit and IMU-based gloves (Parger, et al., 2020)

body.text: Yet, these systems could never be this efficient if it wasn’t for the software that analyses the generated data.
Software appliances

The main challenge that programmers have to face when designing so-called “VR-ready” software, is the need for two points of view, or cameras, one for each eye. This is due to the fact that our perception of depth is highly dependent on our ability to merge two slightly different images, allowing us to see both sides of an object at the same time when it is close to us.

The drastically different interface, when comparing a headset to a common computer monitor also requires many modifications in terms of user interface, but also of sound quality and graphics. Rendering techniques such as caustic shading (Négrel-Jerzy, 2022) or ray tracing may be implemented with the aim to improve the realism of an environment in which the user is supposed to feel immersed.
Conclusion

The emergence of fully virtual worlds such as the metaverse by Meta (formerly Facebook) shows the increasing importance of VR in our lives, sometimes without the need for special gear: augmented reality is slowly making its way into our daily routines, mostly through some of our smartphone applications. This technology is constantly evolving, breakthroughs are being made every day, improving both its looks and its performance. And yet, this persistent seeking of innovation and progress has been proven to be our society’s main vulnerability. With climate change on our doorstep, should we really keep on following such an ethically unacceptable industrial model? It is to be hopped that we will eventually learn from our mistakes, and save ourselves from the consequences of our own choices.

poems.title: Crépuscule grec
poems.summary: Sur un banc, face aux rochers qui coiffent le village, la lumière de midi change un visage aimé en statue.

stanzas: Ce matin les toits brillent,
inondés de soleil.
Sur les coteaux vermeils
des enfants s'éparpillent.
Couronnant le village telle une mitre grise,
des massifs rocheux dominent l'horizon.
Et du haut de leurs cimes embrumées, le gazon
déverse sa verdure sur un clocher d'église.
Depuis un banc, assis, je contemple la vue.
Je savoure ce calme solennel que parfois
ponctuent les tons joyeux de ses rires, de sa voix.
Les yeux rivés sur ce spectacle imprévu,
je caresse sa main. Mes démons se sont tus,
comme attendris peut-être, par la splendeur profonde
de ce moment de paix et d'amour impromptu.
Il est bientôt midi, la lumière furibonde
donne à ses traits marbrés des reflets de statue.

poems.title: Forêt dansante
poems.summary: Sous les chênes d'argent, un acrobate danse sur sa corde et seul le ciel l'applaudit.

stanzas: Lourde est la corde et brave est l'habile acrobate
sous les chênes d'argent, il s'élance, gracieux
du feuillage rayonne un soleil écarlate
seuls témoins de l'exploit, s'émerveillent les cieux

poems.title: L'exil
poems.summary: Une dernière nuit dans un Paris endeuillé, avant que l'aube n'emporte la ville et les rêves d'enfant.

stanzas: Ce soir la ville est morne, les arbres sont en deuil.
Les carreaux larmoyants ont des teintes bleuâtres.
Pourtant, aucun passant ne pleure, aucun cercueil
dans les rues désertées d'un Paris acariâtre.
Ce teint sombre et muet, ce silence morose,
il trouve son ardeur dans mon esprit hagard.
Pour l'apaiser, tantôt j'ai couché ci ma prose
mais elle ne peut défaire mes chaînes. Je m'égare
dans les traits dilués par les larmes versées.
Bientôt je partirai, et mes rêves d'enfants
resteront tous ici. Et c'est le cœur gercé
que je m'assoupirai à l'aube, caressant
d'une main frémissante, le velours des fauteuils.
Un son strident retentira, note angoissante,
glas sourd annonçant mon exil; en un clin d'œil
les balustrades, les toitures grises opalescentes
seront déjà perdues dans la brume aurorale.

poems.title: Le comédien
poems.summary: Un comédien d'improvisation voit surgir de la brume un cavalier d'ombre, et lui répond par la foudre.

stanzas: Sur la scène embrumée d'illusions impalpables
se dresse un comédien, emblème du chaos.
De son esprit radieux, ruissellent quelques fables
mais nul ne voit vraiment, de fin à son propos.
C'est néanmoins sans but, étourdi formidable,
qu'il déclame fièrement sa tirade, et là-haut
sa muse, divertie, cache d'un air affable
la clé tant convoitée du trésor qu'est l'impro.
Mais voilà que des brumes indéfinies, macabres
se dessine soudain, l'ombre d'un cavalier
sa monture invisible, frémit, hennit, se cabre
et lacère le brouillard de ses sabots d'acier.
Le comédien frissonne, mais se pare au combat
des éclairs jaillissent de ses mains argentées.
Le premier coup est sien, et de ses feux l'éclat
n'a d'égal ici bas que sa dextérité.

poems.title: Les pèlerins du rail
poems.summary: Un train glisse sur Paris, du couchant de rubis à la torpeur de la nuit, et berce ses pèlerins endormis.

stanzas: La ville est assoupie, le soleil est de glace
Des reflets palpitants sur les vitres du train
s'élèvent des figures, sombres, et c'est l'audace
de l'habile architecte, artiste dont l'entrain
a su mouvoir des villes, fédérer des génies
qui défie, souveraine, l'horizon monotone
d'un Paris dont Montmartre est le seul insoumis.
Le ciel est de rubis, comme en un soir d'automne.
Nuit d'été, chaleur sourde, aux couleurs estompées
Lueurs mourantes et mornes, baignant de leurs pénombre
le satin suranné des rideaux déchirés
Ronflement monotone, murmure perdu dans l'ombre
des passagers bercés par la voie délabrée.

poems.title: Ode au désert
poems.summary: Une piste de terre ensablée, et des phares qui peinent à percer un crépuscule pourpre.

stanzas: Sur ce chemin terreux perdu dans le lointain,
à travers des torrents et des falaises antiques,
l'herbe courbe l'échine, et les vents incertains
caressent la dentelle infinie et lithique
des berges désolées de ce désert brumeux.
Parmi les roches ocres, nul être ne subsiste,
et seul le sable blanc, aux reflets résineux,
tourbillonne en silence, et recouvre la piste.
La route est longue, hélas ! Pourpre est le crépuscule.
Les phares scintillants du monstre de métal
peinent à révéler les arbres minuscules
cernant le précipice de sinistres pétales.

poems.title: Pénombre d'été
poems.summary: Un soleil hésitant strie la chambre : un dormeur sourit à son reflet, tandis qu'elle rit, debout comme une idole.

stanzas: Enseveli, rêveur, parmi les draps de nacre,
il observe ahuri, arborant un sourire,
son reflet translucide dans le miroir de cire
aux teintes grisonnantes, emplies de senteurs âcres.
Des stores bancals au bois fendu, irrégulier,
se déverse un soleil hésitant et fugace.
Il répand sur les murs sa chevelure de glace
et strie de son chaos la pièce immaculée.
Rayonnante de joie, le visage radiant,
elle se dresse dans l'ombre telle une idole antique
et s'esclaffe d'un rire aux timbres idylliques,
admirant, inlassable, son accomplissement.

poems.title: The enslaved acrobat
poems.summary: A prisoner rushes into battle and hovers like a ghost over the fallen, until the night claims him too.

stanzas: Rundown gears rumble in the night,
weeping engines covered in tears and dust.
The prisoner rushes into the fight,
his mind is weak and overcome with rust.
The ground is harsh and unforgiving;
under the sand, lie the defeated,
their daggers raised below, their king
perished at their side, beheaded.
Yet the prisoner's feet fly above
like a ghostly bird, he hovers
upon the moonlit pond where love's
only presence is scattered clovers.
The field is cold, the moon is bright
a drop of blood has stained the moss.
Another life is claimed tonight
the prisoner has joined the lost.

poems.summary: A stranger in a lakeside town at night, deciphering an unknown tongue and looking for the place where heaven never ends.
